Timestamp-based stream processing is available in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. There is no additional charge for this feature beyond standard GetRecords API request charges. To get started, see Amazon DynamoDB Streams timestamp documentation in the DynamoDB developer guide.

title: Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API
body: Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports the Kubernetes Gateway API, giving customers a standard, portable way to define how traffic reaches their applications. Customers can configure application load balancing using Gateway and HTTPRoute resources, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS infrastructure automatically. With this launch, EKS Auto Mode customers can adopt the next-generation Kubernetes traffic management standard without installing or configuring a separate controller. Capabilities include HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace traffic routing for multi-team environments, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager. Existing workloads using Ingress resources continue to work alongside Gateway API resources. To get started, see the Amazon EKS documentation . Gateway API support is included as part of EKS Auto Mode and is available in all AWS Regions where EKS Auto Mode is supported. Standard charges apply for the AWS load balancing resources provisioned.

title: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey introduces ElastiCache Insights
body: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now features ElastiCache Insights, a pre-built dashboard in Amazon CloudWatch for your node-based clusters. ElastiCache Insights brings cluster health, memory, compute, network, command throughput, latency, keyspace, and errors into a single view sourced from a set of OpenTelemetry metrics that ElastiCache publishes automatically. You can use ElastiCache Insights to check the health of your cache workloads across a Region at a glance, detect when a node nears its memory, network, or connection limits, and filter your view to a cluster, shard, node, or Availability Zone. You can also save a copy as the starting point for a custom dashboard tailored to your workload. With detailed monitoring, you can choose metrics to publish every 15 seconds and view them on the Metrics tab or in your custom dashboard. CloudWatch pricing for OpenTelemetry metrics applies to ElastiCache detailed monitoring. To get started, open the Metrics tab for a cluster in the Amazon ElastiCache console and choose View in ElastiCache Insights. You can also choose ElastiCache Insights under Infrastructure Monitoring in the Amazon CloudWatch console. ElastiCache Insights is available for node-based Valkey clusters in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. To learn more about ElastiCache Insights, see Monitoring ElastiCache with OpenTelemetry metrics in the Amazon ElastiCache User Guide.

title: Amazon EMR Serverless now supports IPv6 and dual-stack connectivity
body: Amazon EMR Serverless now supports IPv6 and dual-stack connectivity, expanding beyond the IPv4-only connectivity that was previously available. You can now run your Apache Spark and Apache Hive jobs over IPv6 in your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) by supplying dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6) or IPv6-only subnets. This gives you greater flexibility in how your applications connect to data stores and services, while maintaining full backward compatibility with your existing IPv4 workloads. As Spark and Hive workloads scale to many workers, the IPv4 address space in your VPCs and subnets can become a constraint, and a growing number of organizations face compliance mandates that require IPv6 adoption. With dual-stack connectivity, your EMR Serverless applications accept both IPv4 and IPv6, making it easy to adopt IPv6 gradually while maintaining backward compatibility with your existing IPv4 workloads. With IPv6-only subnets, you can eliminate the need for IPv4 addresses entirely, overcoming IPv4 address exhaustion and meeting the networking standards and compliance requirements that call for IPv6, while your jobs reach IPv6 endpoints and services both inside and outside your VPC. IPv6 and dual-stack connectivity for Amazon EMR Serverless is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where Amazon EMR Serverless is available. IPv6 and dual-stack subnets are supported on all EMR Serverless release versions. To get started, see Configure IPv6 subnets for EMR Serverless applications and Configuring VPC access for EMR Serverless applications .

title: Amazon Location Service launches an interactive API Playground featuring Places, Routes and Maps APIs
body: Amazon Location Service now offers a complete, interactive API Playground that lets developers explore and test every Places, Routes, and Maps API visually without writing code. With this release, all 14 Amazon Location Service Places, Maps and Routes APIs are available in an interactive API Playground, where developers can make real API calls, see results rendered on an interactive map, adjust parameters, and copy ready-to-use request snippets directly into their applications. The API Playground covers Amazon Location Service's Places, Routes, and Maps APIs: search and geocoding (Geocode, ReverseGeocode, Autocomplete, Suggest, SearchText, SearchNearby, and GetPlace), route planning and optimization (CalculateRoutes, CalculateRouteMatrix, CalculateIsolines, OptimizeWaypoints, and SnapToRoads), and mapping (Dynamic Map and GetStaticMap). Customers can simulate validating delivery addresses, planning truck-safe multi-stop routes, visualizing drive-time service areas, or embedding maps into their apps — with no SDK setup or test scripts required. The API Playground is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (Ohio), US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), and South America (São Paulo). To get started, visit the Amazon Location Service API Playground in the AWS Console, or learn more in the Developer Guide .

title: Announcing Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic with improved reasoning for voice agents
body: Today, we announce the general availability of Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, our latest speech-to-speech model for natural, real-time voice agents. This release brings improved reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling accuracy to real-time voice applications. The model also delivers lower latency, enabling faster, more natural interactions. Nova 2.5 Sonic helps voice agents maintain context, follow multi-step instructions, and use connected tools to complete customer tasks. For example, a customer-service agent can look up an order, check return eligibility, and initiate a return within a conversation. These improvements help developers build more capable voice agents for customer service, personal AI assistants, and real-time conversational applications. Nova 2.5 Sonic builds on existing capabilities, including robust speech understanding, expressive voices in seven languages, and controllable turn-taking, alongside support for voice and text in the same session, asynchronous tool calling, and a 256K context window. Developers can also use Nova 2.5 Sonic with Strands Bidi Agents, now generally available, to build production voice agents in a few lines of code, with longer conversations and connections to other agents. Nova 2.5 Sonic is available in Amazon Bedrock in the US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) AWS Regions, at the same pricing as Nova 2 Sonic. To learn more, visit the Amazon Nova models page . To get started, see the Amazon Nova user guide , and blog on building voice agents with Nova 2.5 Sonic and Strands Bidi Agents .

title: Amazon Q Developer now delivers enhanced visualizations in the AWS Management Console
body: Today, AWS announces enhanced visualization for Amazon Q Developer in the AWS Management Console. Amazon Q now reasons across hundreds of AWS APIs to answer complex questions and deliver complete answers about your entire account—across all regions and services. Beyond the resource tables and cost charts introduced earlier this year, Amazon Q now renders health dashboards with status indicators, time-series charts with trend and anomaly detection, troubleshooting diagnostics, and resource detail views. Previously, asking “Show me the health of my production environment” returned a text summary that customers had to read line by line. Today, Amazon Q orchestrates calls across multiple services, gathers health data, and renders a dashboard with status indicators—giving customers a complete picture at a glance. Similarly, “Graph network utilization for my EC2 instances over 12 hours” now generates an interactive time-series chart with trend lines and anomaly highlighting —making it faster to spot issues and take action. These responses are also noticeably faster, so customers get complete answers in seconds rather than waiting on multi-step, text-only replies. To use Amazon Q in the AWS Management Console, click on the Q icon on the top left after you sign-in to the AWS Management Console. Enhanced visualization features for Amazon Q Developer are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Q Developer is available . To learn more, see the Amazon Q Developer documentation.

title: Amazon S3 Tables now support up to 100 table buckets per AWS Region in an AWS account
body: Amazon S3 Tables now support up to 100 table buckets per AWS Region in an AWS account, increased from 10. This allows you to create up to 1 million tables per AWS Region in an AWS account. With a higher table bucket allowance, you can create a separate table bucket for each dataset, workload, or team, and apply table bucket-level settings such as encryption, access policies, and replication to each. The higher quota applies by default to all accounts at no additional cost. S3 Tables deliver the first cloud object store with built-in Apache Iceberg support, and the easiest way to store tabular data at scale. S3 Tables perform continual table maintenance to automatically optimize query efficiency and storage cost over time, even as your data lake scales and evolves. The higher default quota is available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables are available. If you need a quota beyond the default, you can request an increase through AWS Support. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables overview page , user guide , and quotas documentation .

title: Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances now supports ModifyVolume API
body: Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances now supports the ModifyVolume API, which lets you change volume size, volume type, IOPS, or throughput in place, without detaching the volume or restarting the instance. Previously, changing storage capacity or performance on a deployed managed instance required rebuilding it. With ModifyVolume, you can increase volume size up to 16,384 GiB, switch between supported Amazon EBS volume types, adjust IOPS for gp3, io1, and io2 volumes, and modify throughput for gp3 volumes. The API supports idempotency tokens to prevent duplicate changes, and you can track progress with the Amazon EC2 DescribeVolumesModifications operation. ModifyVolume is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances is available. To get started, call ModifyVolume directly, or use it through your WorkSpaces Core partner solution once available. To learn more, see ModifyVolume in the WorkSpaces Instances API Reference and Limitations in the Amazon EBS User Guide, or visit WorkSpaces Core .

title: Amazon Aurora serverless now supports up to 384 ACUs
body: Amazon Aurora serverless now supports database capacity of up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition, a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU provides approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory with corresponding CPU and networking, so a single Aurora serverless database can now scale up to 768 GiB of memory. When the workload completes, Aurora serverless automatically scales down to zero. This makes Aurora serverless especially well-suited for agentic AI applications, which typically have bursts of activity, long idle windows, and unpredictable traffic patterns. Aurora serverless handles all of it automatically, scaling capacity with your agents, so you only pay for what you use. With 384 ACU support, customers can now use Aurora serverless for even more demanding workloads while continuing to scale down to zero when not in use, paying only for the capacity consumed. For new clusters, select a supported Aurora PostgreSQL engine version and set your maximum capacity up to 384 ACUs. For existing clusters on Platform Version 4, simply modify the cluster to update the maximum capacity setting (and the engine version if needed). There will be no downtime if your database is already on Platform Version 4. For existing clusters on older platform versions, upgrade to Platform Version 4 through a pending maintenance action. 384 ACU support is available for Aurora PostgreSQL versions 18.4, 17.10, 16.14, 15.18, and 14.23, running on Platform Version 4. To learn more, see Aurora serverless capacity in the Amazon Aurora User Guide. For pricing details and Region availability, visit Amazon Aurora Pricing . To get started, create or modify an Aurora serverless database in the AWS Management Console .

title: AWS announces TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch Support for AWS Trainium (Public Beta)
body: Today, AWS launched the public beta of TorchNeuron, an open source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium. Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed to deliver high performance and cost efficiency for deep learning AI training and inference workloads. TorchNeuron enables AI scientists and researchers to experiment and build models with PyTorch natively on Trainium. With TorchNeuron, developers can enable their PyTorch code on Trainium simply by switching to .to('neuron') while maintaining full PyTorch compatibility with eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. TorchNeuron is available as open source through the TorchNeuron github repo for Amazon EC2 Trainium2 instances and Amazon EC2 Trainium3 instances. To learn more about TorchNeuron and AWS Trainium accelerators, visit the AWS Neuron page .

title: AWS Batch now supports Amazon EKS access entry authentication
body: AWS Batch now supports Amazon EKS access entry authentication for compute environments. EKS access entries provide an API-driven approach to granting IAM principals access to Kubernetes clusters, complementing the existing aws-auth ConfigMap . AWS Batch can now authenticate to your cluster through the access entry mechanism, simplifying cluster setup and authentication lifecycle management. To get started, use the CreateComputeEnvironment or UpdateComputeEnvironment APIs to set accessEntry.desiredState to ENABLED on all AWS Batch compute environments targeting your cluster. AWS Batch creates one access entry per cluster and associates the AWSBatchClusterPolicy with it. You can configure access entries through the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS Management Console. Access entry authentication for AWS Batch on Amazon EKS is now supported in all AWS Regions where AWS Batch is available. For more information, see Amazon EKS access entry authentication in the AWS Batch User Guide .

title: AWS Brazil automates distribution of non-Brazilian software product licenses to Brazilian customers
body: AWS Brazil now provides an automated distribution workflow through the AWS Brazil 2P Distribution Program. Eligible non-Brazilian independent software vendors (ISVs) grant AWS Brazil the right to distribute their Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) product licenses, and AWS Brazil distributes them to customers in Brazil. AWS Brazil is the seller of record, invoicing Brazilian customers in Brazilian Reais (BRL) with applicable Brazilian taxes. The distribution authorizations, seller disbursements, withholding tax calculation, invoicing, and seller reporting are automated. Eligible ISVs agree to the applicable Brazil 2P distribution terms to grant AWS Brazil the right to distribute SaaS product licenses locally by creating distribution authorizations through AWS Partner Central or public APIs. AWS Brazil, as the seller of record, creates private offers for Brazilian buyers, determines the buyer-facing price, and automatically generates invoices, calculates and withholds taxes, and disburses payments. ISVs track transactions and payment status through the Seller Insights dashboard. Buyers in Brazil see private offers priced in USD and invoiced in BRL by AWS Brazil, using the exchange rate on the invoice date. Buyers can pay by credit card (Visa, Mastercard, American Express) or Pay by Invoice (PBI), add a purchase order number, and access invoices in the AWS Billing Console. To learn more about the AWS Brazil 2P Distribution Program, visit the AWS Marketplace Seller Guide and the AWS Marketplace Buyer Guide .

title: AWS Client VPN now supports device posture assessment
body: AWS Client VPN now supports device posture assessment, allowing you to verify that connecting user devices meet your security and compliance requirements before granting network access. This feature integrates with your existing device posture providers, so only trusted, compliant devices can access your AWS resources through Client VPN. Previously, Client VPN authenticated users through certificates, SAML, or Active Directory. With device posture assessment, you can now also integrate CrowdStrike , Jamf , or JumpCloud with Client VPN to automatically evaluate device security signals such as compliance scores, encryption status, and risk level before allowing a connection. You define these requirements using Cedar policies , giving you fine-grained control over which devices can connect. To help you author and validate these policies, Client VPN provides you a Test Policy tool that guides you through creating Cedar policies for your device posture requirements. This feature continuously re-evaluates device compliance during active sessions, and automatically disconnects a session if a device falls out of compliance, such as when risk score or security settings change. You can also use this feature in monitoring-only mode, which logs posture evaluation results without disconnecting sessions, so you can assess the impact of your policies before enforcing them. Device posture assessment works alongside your existing authorization rules to provide defense in depth. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Client VPN is available, at no additional cost. This feature requires AWS VPN Client version 6.2.0 or later. To learn more about Client VPN: Visit the AWS Client VPN product page Download the AWS VPN Client Read the AWS Client VPN administrator guide Read the AWS Client VPN user guide

title: AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing now supports continuous penetration testing integrated directly into your CI/CD pipeline
body: AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing now integrates continuous penetration testing directly into your CI/CD pipeline (public preview) AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing (formerly AWS Security Agent) already provides continuous, on-demand penetration testing without the need to contract third-party pentest vendors. Now, in public preview, Continuum for Penetration Testing shifts security testing even further left by integrating directly into your existing CI/CD systems, making penetration testing a deploy-time event. Development teams ship code daily, but even with on-demand penetration testing available, security validation often happens outside the deployment workflow. CI/CD integration closes this gap. Developers receive findings, including severity, affected endpoints, and remediation guidance, directly in pipeline output. Non-security changes complete with no meaningful delay, and the pipeline automatically re-tests and verifies fixes after remediation without requiring manual re-triggers. Getting started requires no security expertise. An auto-generated pipeline snippet can be pasted into any existing pipeline and is completable in under five minutes. Application context bootstraps automatically on the first run, with no prior full penetration test required. Continuous penetration testing is available today. To get started, visit our documentation .

title: AWS End User Messaging adds a guided wizard for RCS registration videos
body: Today, AWS End User Messaging adds a wizard that orchestrates the entire video capture for your RCS agent registration. RCS registrations in multiple countries, including the United States, require a screen recording that demonstrates your messaging experience. To record it, you have to send a specific sequence of messages to a test device, and until now you scripted those messages yourself, which easily introduced errors and made a mismatched or incomplete video one of the hardest parts of registering for RCS. The wizard now drives each step of the capture for you, sending the right messages in the right order, so you record a compliant video the first time and get your agent approved sooner. The wizard is on all RCS registration forms that require a video submission. To learn more and get started, see the AWS End User Messaging User Guide.

title: AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports table optimization, statistics, and crawlers for Apache Iceberg V3
body: AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports table optimization, statistics, and crawlers for Apache Iceberg Version 3 (V3) tables. With these new capabilities, you can automatically maintain V3 tables, optimize them for query performance, and discover them in Amazon S3. With table optimization, you can compact V3 tables using binpack, sort, or z-order strategies to improve query performance, and remove expired snapshots and orphan files to reduce storage costs. These optimizations support V3 data types, including variant, geospatial, and nanosecond-precision timestamps. You can also generate number of distinct values (NDV) statistics for V3 tables, which analytics engines use to plan queries efficiently. In addition, you can use Glue crawlers to discover V3 tables stored in Amazon S3 and register them in Glue Data Catalog, making them available to query with any V3-compatible engines. These capabilities are available for Iceberg V3 tables in all AWS Regions where Glue Data Catalog table optimization, statistics, and crawlers are available. To learn more, see Glue Optimization , Glue Statistics , and Glue crawlers in the Glue Developer Guide.

title: AWS HealthOmics introduces resource fallback order for Nextflow workflows
body: Today, AWS HealthOmics introduces the resource fallback directive for tasks in your Nextflow workflows, enabling you to define an ordered list of preferred accelerator types, including an option to fallback to CPU instances. Researchers and bioinformaticians can use this directive to reduce time spent diagnosing and resubmitting runs due to accelerator constraints and keep production workflows running. AWS HealthOmics is a HIPAA-eligible service that helps healthcare and life sciences customers accelerate scientific breakthroughs at scale with fully managed bioinformatics workflows. With resource fallback for Nextflow workflows, you can prioritize your preferred accelerator for your task. When your preferred accelerator is unavailable, HealthOmics automatically moves through your specified alternatives in the fallback without resubmission. Each accelerator profile has a configurable timeout, giving you control over how long HealthOmics searches for that accelerator before moving to the next. Shorter timeouts help you move quickly through the fallback order, while longer timeouts increase the probability of reserving your preferred accelerator. You can also include a CPU profile as a final fallback to increase the likelihood of your task reserving an instance. You can now use resource fallback for Nextflow workflows in all AWS HealthOmics Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London), Israel (Tel Aviv), and Asia Pacific (Seoul, Singapore, Tokyo). To learn more, visit the advanced resource configuration and Nextflow specifics documentation.

title: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports network access controls for Identity Store
body: AWS IAM Identity Center helps you configure the single sign-on experience for your workforce to AWS accounts and applications. IAM Identity Center now supports network access controls for Identity Store, which stores your users and groups. You can restrict access to the Identity Store API and the SCIM API based on the network that requests originate from. Your custom applications and user provisioning workflows use the Identity Store API to manage and look up users and groups, and your external identity provider uses the SCIM API to synchronize users and groups. For the Identity Store API, you can require that requests arrive only through allowed VPC endpoints in your account or organization, or from specific source VPCs. For both APIs, you can allow requests only from specific IP ranges. Within the same configuration, you can apply different restrictions to each API. For example, you can require that Identity Store API requests arrive only through VPC endpoints, while allowing SCIM requests from your external identity provider's published IP ranges. Network access controls are optional and turned off by default. Requests that AWS services make on your behalf are exempt. You configure network access controls by using the Identity Store API through the AWS SDKs and AWS CLI. This capability is available in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is offered. To learn more about IAM Identity Center, visit the product detail page . To get started with network access controls, see the Identity Store API Reference .

title: AWS Lambda announces Lambda Web Functions
body: AWS Lambda announces Lambda Web Functions, a new serverless compute primitive where your code handles HTTP requests directly. Your code listens on a port and handles requests as it would on any HTTP server. You use frameworks you already know, such as Express or Hono, with no adapters or custom configuration. This enables you to serve workloads such as AI inference endpoints, server-side rendered (SSR) web apps, streaming API endpoints, microservices, and webhooks. You pay for active CPU time and the memory your environment holds, not for idle CPU time your code spends waiting on databases or downstream services. With this launch, we are also renaming existing Lambda functions to Lambda Event Functions, a naming change only that requires no code changes or redeployments for your existing functions. Builders use Lambda to go from code to production quickly and without managing servers, across event-driven pipelines, request-response APIs, and data processing. As AI-driven development accelerates, they want to build locally and deploy with a familiar programming model and pay for workloads based on active CPU usage, while serving users with low latency. Lambda Web Functions delivers this. Today, Lambda Web Functions supports the Node.js runtime. A single warm execution environment can serve multiple concurrent requests, which reduces cold starts by orders of magnitude. You can stream results to clients incrementally with native HTTP streaming. You can create and configure Lambda Web Functions using the AWS Lambda API, Agent Toolkit for AWS , AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS SAM, AWS CDK, or the AWS SDKs. With multi-Region routing, you can deploy once and serve each request from the Region closest to the end user. Web Functions support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC. Lambda Web Functions is available today in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). For the current list, see the AWS Capabilities by Region page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions developer guide . For pricing details, see AWS Lambda Pricing . To see Lambda Web Functions in action, see the AWS News Blog announcement .

title: AWS Private CA now provides detailed certificate issuance logs
body: AWS Private CA announces detailed certificate issuance logs, a new AWS CloudTrail service event that records the complete certificate content, issuing CA information, requester identity, and signing status for every issuance. You can use these events for compliance auditing, certificate inventory, algorithm migration tracking, and failed-issuance monitoring. Previously, the CloudTrail management event for the IssueCertificate API confirmed that the API call succeeded by providing a certificate ARN but did not capture the certificate content, information about the CA that signed it, or issuances that failed before signing. The new IssueCertificateDetails event captures the complete to-be-signed (TBS) certificate with all X.509 fields and extensions, plus convenience fields for the subject, issuer, serial number, validity period, template, and signing algorithm. Events are emitted for both successful and failed issuance, so pre-signing failures such as name constraints violations now produce a record with a failure explanation. Each event identifies the requester: the account and IAM principal for direct API callers, or the service principal for certificates issued through AWS Private CA connectors or integrated AWS services. In cross-account configurations, the event is delivered to the CA owner account. The event is delivered automatically as a CloudTrail management event, with no configuration or opt-in required and no additional cost beyond standard AWS CloudTrail pricing. Because it flows through CloudTrail, you can act on it in real time with Amazon EventBridge or query it in batch with Amazon Athena for certificate auditing, inventory, tracking, and monitoring. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Private CA is offered. To learn more, see the AWS Private CA User Guide .

title: AWS Service Reference Information now supports global condition keys, service names, and data plane classification
body: AWS is expanding programmatic service reference information to help you automate IAM policy management and keep your policies aligned with the latest service updates. The service reference now includes all aws:-prefixed global condition keys in a single machine-readable file, a ServiceName field mapping service identifiers to human-readable names, and an IsDataPlane property identifying which actions are data plane operations. You can automate retrieval of this information to eliminate manual effort, and incorporate it directly into your existing policy management tools and processes. This feature is available at no additional cost. To get started, refer to the documentation on programmatic service reference information .

title: AWS Transform now builds new networks and modernizes security groups
body: AWS Transform for migrations now gives you three ways to bring your network to AWS. In addition to migrating and modernizing your existing network, you can build a new network from scratch or convert your on-premises access rules into optimized security groups and deploy them into existing VPCs. Whichever path you choose, you arrive on AWS with a secure and scalable network foundation. On-premises networks accumulate years of definitions and access rules that you may not want to carry to AWS as-is. For a clean start, AWS Transform builds a new network aligned to AWS best practices. To bring your access rules with you, AWS Transform converts them into security groups and modernizes them as it goes, detecting stale rules and recommending optimizations, then deploys the groups into your existing VPCs without redeploying your network stack. These capabilities allow you migrate to any AWS commercial or GovCloud Region . To get started, see Migrate networks . To learn more, visit AWS Transform for migrations .

title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails now supports Standard tier for contextual grounding checks
body: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails now offers a Standard tier for contextual grounding checks, which detect and filter hallucinations by checking whether a model response is grounded in your reference source and relevant to the user's query. The Standard tier is more robust than the Classic tier. It supports responses that include reasoning or conversational content, scores differently worded responses with the same meaning more consistently, and provides more comprehensive language support, matching the Standard tier for content filters and denied topics. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable safeguards for generative AI applications on any foundation model through the ApplyGuardrail API. Until now, contextual grounding checks applied strict grounding suited to summarization, paraphrasing, and question answering. With the Standard tier, you can also apply contextual grounding checks to conversational applications and to responses that reason over the source. You choose the tier for each guardrail in the Amazon Bedrock console or API. Existing guardrails keep the Classic tier until you change them. Pricing is the same for both tiers. To use the Standard tier, your guardrail must use cross-Region inference with a guardrail profile. The Standard tier for contextual grounding checks is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (Milan), Europe (Paris), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails documentation on contextual grounding checks and safeguard tiers , or visit the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails product page .

title: Amazon Braket now in scope for FedRAMP Class C
body: Amazon Braket is now in scope for FedRAMP Class C in AWS US Regions where Braket is available. The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) is a US government-wide program that delivers a standard approach to the security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring of cloud products and services. With FedRAMP Class C authorization, government customers and the organizations that serve them can use Amazon Braket to explore quantum computing within an authorized boundary. The AWS-operated components of Braket, including the API and SDK, job orchestration and management, compilation, and result storage in Amazon S3, are within the FedRAMP-certified boundary, while quantum workloads execute on third-party Quantum Hardware Providers (QHPs) outside that boundary. All data sent to QHPs meets AWS' privacy and security requirements including removal of all personally identifiable information, data encryption in transit and at rest, and adherence to AWS' standard data retention and deletion policies. To learn more about FedRAMP, visit AWS FedRAMP services and the FedRAMP Marketplace. To learn more about Amazon Braket, visit the Braket product page and Getting Started on Braket resources. Regional Availability: US East (N. Virginia), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon)

title: Amazon Bedrock now offers Canada cross-Region inference for Claude Haiku 5.5
body: Amazon Bedrock now offers Canada cross-Region inference (CRIS) for Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5. Customers with strict data residency requirements can now keep inference processing entirely within Canada. Canada CRIS routes requests only between ca-central-1 (Canada Central) and ca-west-1 (Canada West, Calgary). This helps organizations in financial services, healthcare, the public sector, and other regulated industries meet federal and provincial data residency requirements. Canada CRIS adds to the inference options already available to customers in Canada. US CRIS and global CRIS remain fully supported for Claude Haiku 5.5. Both route requests across a broader set of AWS Regions, and global CRIS also offers cost savings, which makes these options a good fit for workloads that don't require inference processing to stay in Canada. Canada CRIS is designated as an inference profile with limited model selection. Future models and model versions might not be released for this profile. We recommend Canada CRIS for workloads that must keep inference processing within Canada. For more details, see Inference profiles with limited model selection in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For the most current information about model availability in each Region, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To get started with Claude models on Amazon Bedrock, visit the Amazon Bedrock console.

title: Amazon CloudFront announces dual-stack support for VPC origins
body: Amazon CloudFront now supports end-to-end IPv6 delivery to origins inside your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with the new dual-stack VPC origins. With VPC origins, customers keep their Application Load Balancers (ALB), Network Load Balancers (NLB), and EC2 instances in private subnets that only their CloudFront distributions can reach. With dual-stack support, customers can now send IPv6 traffic all the way to these private origins to meet their IPv6 architecture and regulatory requirements, without exposing origins to the internet. Previously, CloudFront supported dual-stack for public origins but connected to VPC origins over IPv4 only. Customers faced a tradeoff: move origins to public subnets for IPv6 and give up VPC origin security or keep them private and stay on IPv4. Now, with this launch, customers can configure their VPC origins as dual-stack and get end-to-end IPv6 without sacrificing security. Dual-stack VPC origins are available in all AWS Commercial Regions where VPC origins are supported. The full list of supported Regions is available here . There is no additional cost for using dual-stack VPC origins. To learn more, visit CloudFront VPC origins.

title: Amazon Connect Customer now measures the outcomes that drive retention and revenue
body: Amazon Connect Customer now scores the outcome of your customer interactions. It shows whether the customer left satisfied, is at risk of churning, made a purchase, or resolved their need in self-service. You can now see whether an interaction worked, not just how efficiently it ran. Each metric comes with a default definition you can adjust to match how your business defines success and are available both through the analytics dashboards and APIs.

title: Amazon Connect Customer launches two new layouts for agent workspace
body: Amazon Connect Customer now offers two different layouts that optimize screen space on the agent workspace. Contact center agents spend hours each day in the agent workspace, which includes all of the contact controls and applications they need to resolve customer issues. Agents who handle different channels and workflows want the workspace arranged differently, so that they can quickly read, respond, and access their tools. Now, administrators can choose the best layout for each team, maximizing agent efficiency and satisfaction. On the Modern layout, contact controls are at the top of the workspace, maximizing screen space for the applications beneath during voice calls. When agents handle chat, email, and task contacts on the Modern layout, they now have a taller, wider area to read and respond. The Classic layout offers a familiar experience for agents already using the agent workspace, now with contact controls that expand and contract by channel and a resizable agent assist application. Administrators can assign the Modern layout to a team migrating from another agent desktop with controls at the top, while teams already familiar with the agent workspace can use the Classic layout. You can use the new layouts for the Amazon Connect Customer agent workspace in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London). To learn more and get started, see the agent workspace in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

title: AWS DataSync Enhanced mode now supports FSx for OpenZFS, NFS 4.2, and object metadata controls
body: AWS DataSync Enhanced mode now supports Amazon FSx for OpenZFS as a source or destination location, NFS version 4.2 for on-premises NFS servers and FSx for OpenZFS file systems, and a new ObjectMetadata option for object storage transfers. Previously, customers transferring data to or from FSx for OpenZFS were limited to Basic mode. NFS 4.2 lets you transfer data from NFS servers on the latest version without reconfiguring them to an older protocol version. The ObjectMetadata option gives you control over whether an object's user metadata is copied to the destination, which helps when destination metadata must stay intact, such as buckets served by AWS Storage Gateway, or when source metadata keys are not compatible with the destination, such as Azure Blob Storage. Existing tasks remain unaffected and continue to run as scheduled. These capabilities are available for Enhanced mode tasks in all AWS Regions where AWS DataSync Enhanced mode is supported. To learn more, visit the AWS DataSync documentation .

title: Amazon EC2 introduces shared tags for Amazon Machine Images
body: Amazon EC2 now supports AMI tag sharing, a new feature that lets AMI owners make selected tags visible to all AWS accounts an AMI is shared with. Whether an AMI is shared with an account, across an organization, or made public, a shared tag is automatically shared alongside the AMI, eliminating the need to build and maintain custom tag replication workflows. AMI owners simply add the 'ec2:SharedTag/' prefix to any tag key, and every account the AMI is shared with can immediately see it. This removes the operational burden of replicating tags into each account after sharing an AMI. Shared tags are read-only for recipient accounts, so only the owner can create, modify, or delete them. They count only against the owner's 50 tag per resource quota, allowing recipient accounts to continue adding their own private tags without any impact to their limits. This feature is available in all AWS Regions at no additional cost. To learn more, please visit the documentation and read the blog .

title: Amazon ECS Managed Instances adds cross-instance and Spot consolidation
body: Today, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Managed Instances introduces two infrastructure optimization updates: cross-instance and Spot consolidation. Cross-instance consolidation evaluates tasks running across multiple underutilized instances together, packing them onto fewer instances to raise utilization and lower costs. Spot consolidation extends this capability to Spot capacity, consolidating underutilized Spot Instances after first verifying replacement capacity is available. Amazon ECS Managed Instances provisions, configures, and operates right-sized Amazon EC2 instances for your workloads, balancing availability and cost. Its infrastructure optimization continuously monitors your fleet, reclaiming idle capacity and consolidating underutilized instances with graceful start-before-stop task replacement. Until now, optimization evaluated each instance in isolation for replacement, which worked well when a capacity provider was configured with diverse instance types. However, when a capacity provider was configured with a narrow range of instance types, there were fewer opportunities to consolidate multiple underutilized instances, because no single replacement could yield savings. With cross-instance consolidation, ECS now evaluates and repacks tasks across multiple instances simultaneously. For example, in our testing with a capacity provider configured for c9g instances with a minimum size of 4xlarge, running 261 tasks (each 1 vCPU, 1.94 GiB), cross-instance consolidation reduced the fleet from 19 instances (seven 4xlarge, seven 8xlarge, four 12xlarge, and one 24xlarge) to 13 instances (eight 4xlarge and five 8xlarge), while raising CPU utilization from 42% to 91% and memory utilization from 41% to 88%. Spot consolidation applies the same approach to Spot capacity, first verifying replacement capacity is available. With these enhancements, ECS Managed Instances delivers deeper cost optimization for both your On-Demand and Spot workloads. Cross-instance and Spot consolidation are now available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions, and apply automatically to all existing and new ECS Managed Instances capacity providers. To learn more, see our documentation .

title: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now supports changing durability on existing clusters
body: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now lets you enable or disable durability on your existing node-based clusters. Previously, you couldn't change the durability configuration of an existing cluster in place. This made it harder to move from caching to persistent data store use cases, or to adapt as your application requirements change. Now you can change durability at any point in your application's lifecycle. You can choose between two durability options: synchronous and asynchronous writes. Synchronous writes persist data across at least two AZs before responding to the client, designed for zero data loss at single-digit millisecond write latency. Asynchronous writes persist data after responding to the client, maintaining microsecond write latency at no additional cost. However, up to 10 seconds of uncommitted data could be lost in the rare event of a failure. Both options maintain microsecond read latency. You can now use ElastiCache for a broader set of use cases beyond caching where data loss is unacceptable such as AI agent long-term memory, AI agent workflow state, knowledge bases for RAG applications, payment tokenization, and real-time inventory management. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where ElastiCache for Valkey 9.0 and later is available. To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS SDK, or AWS CLI. For pricing, see the Amazon ElastiCache pricing page . To learn more, see Durability in the ElastiCache documentation.

title: Amazon GuardDuty now supports centralized management using AWS Organizations declarative policies
body: Amazon GuardDuty now supports AWS Organizations declarative policies, enabling you to centrally enable GuardDuty threat detection across every account and Region in your AWS organization. Using an organization policy, you can now apply a centrally managed GuardDuty enablement configuration. The configuration applies to existing accounts and is automatically maintained as new accounts join your organization. Enabling GuardDuty across all relevant accounts and Regions helps ensure comprehensive threat detection coverage. Previously, keeping enablement aligned across a large multi-account, multi-Region environment meant configuring GuardDuty's enablement settings separately in each Region, which could drift over time. Now you can define a central GuardDuty policy from your delegated administrator account that sets an enablement baseline across your organization (at the organization root, OUs, or individual accounts). The policy supports a default configuration that applies in every Region where GuardDuty is available, as well as per-Region overrides for Regions that require different enablement. Enablement set by a policy cannot be overridden via the GuardDuty console or API. GuardDuty declarative policy support is available in all AWS commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, make sure the delegated administrator has permission to manage GuardDuty policies. Then, sign in to the GuardDuty console and choose Organization policies, or create a policy programmatically using AWS Organizations APIs. To learn more, see Managing accounts using organization policies in the Amazon GuardDuty User Guide and Amazon GuardDuty policies in the AWS Organizations User Guide.

title: AWS IAM Identity Center simplifies identity source changes from Active Directory
body: AWS IAM Identity Center now retains your workforce identities and their assignments when you change your identity source from Active Directory to an external identity provider (IdP), such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, or to the Identity Center directory. Specifically, it preserves your users, groups, group memberships, permission set assignments, and application assignments. Previously, this change required you to recreate them in IAM Identity Center. IAM Identity Center helps you connect your workforce identities to AWS once and manage their access centrally across AWS applications and accounts. When you change your identity source from Active Directory, your existing identity store remains in place, so your users and groups keep the same IDs. As a result, users retain their access to AWS accounts and applications, and policies that reference your user IDs, group IDs, or identity store ID continue to work. To make this change, configure your new identity source with the standard setup required for users to sign in. After the change, your workforce signs in through your dual-stack AWS access portal URL. Changing your identity source in the other direction, to Active Directory, works as before. This feature is available for organization instances of IAM Identity Center in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is available. IAM Identity Center is provided at no additional cost. To get started, navigate to the IAM Identity Center console. For more information, see Change your identity source in the IAM Identity Center User Guide. To learn more about IAM Identity Center, visit the product detail page .

title: AWS Lambda recursive loop detection now supports Amazon EventBridge Custom event buses
body: AWS Lambda recursive loop detection now automatically detects and stops recursive loops between Lambda Event Functions and Amazon EventBridge Custom event buses , helping protect you against unintended usage and unexpected charges from runaway workloads. Lambda recursive loop detection , enabled by default on your AWS account, automatically identifies when a Lambda Event Function is invoked recursively by a supported AWS service and stops the loop. You can use EventBridge Custom event buses to invoke Lambda Event Functions, building automation workflows and scheduling recurring tasks without managing any infrastructure. However, a misconfiguration or code defect can cause EventBridge rules to trigger your Event Functions recursively, resulting in runaway usage. Now, recursive loop detection supports EventBridge Custom buses, automatically stopping such loops and sending you an AWS Health Dashboard notification with troubleshooting instructions. EventBridge Custom event buses now support recursive loop detection in every commercial AWS Region where they are available. This feature is enabled by default on your account and requires no configuration. If your Event Function uses recursive loops intentionally, you can use the PutFunctionRecursionConfig API to turn off recursive loop detection for that function. To learn more about recursive loop detection, visit Lambda documentation .

title: AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router now supports endpoint connection management
body: AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router now supports managing connections through a new endpoint registry, which allows you to register devices or software external to MediaConnect and connect those endpoints to your router inputs and outputs. You can share registered endpoints directly with other AWS accounts, eliminating the need to manually chain router inputs and outputs or coordinate IP addresses and encryption settings out of band. Cross-account endpoint sharing lowers costs by reducing required compute instances and decreases latency through fewer network hops. Sharing is managed through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM), with Connection Manager providing visibility and control over each shared connection. Common use cases include content distributors sharing live feeds with downstream partners, broadcasters collaborating across organizational boundaries, and media workflows that require secure cross-account video transport. MediaConnect endpoint registry is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router is available, at no additional cost. For more information, see the AWS Elemental MediaConnect User Guide .

title: AWS Network Firewall now supports Route 53 Resolved IP Validation
body: AWS Network Firewall now supports IP validation, extending domain-based filtering beyond HTTP/HTTPS to protocols such as SFTP and SSH. This new capability validates that a connection's destination IP address was resolved through your VPC's Amazon Route 53 VPC Resolver, closing security gaps where clients could bypass domain rules. This feature enables Network Firewall customers to implement domain filtering rules for any protocol, not just HTTP/HTTPS, providing more flexible security policies than IP-based rules alone. It simplifies protection against Server Name Identifier (SNI) spoofing by validating the IPs resolved by the Route 53 VPC Resolver against the SNI, ensuring traffic only reaches legitimately resolved destinations. Organizations can now enforce consistent domain-based security policies across all outbound traffic types, from web applications to file transfer protocols, without complex workarounds. Additionally, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall can be used with your VPC Resolver for extended DNS security. Resolved IP validation is available in all AWS commercial regions where AWS Network Firewall and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall are available, at no additional charge. For a full list of supported regions, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page . To learn more, visit AWS Network Firewall product page and service documentation .

title: OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol now supports Ultrafast mode on Amazon Bedrock
body: Today, AWS announces the availability of Ultrafast mode for GPT-6.1 Sol from OpenAI on Amazon Bedrock. Ultrafast mode provides faster inference for workloads where speed matters most. The Amazon Bedrock inference engine delivers the performance, security, and reliability required for production workloads. Use GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast for latency-sensitive applications such as real-time coding assistants, interactive agents, and customer-facing experiences that require fast, high-quality responses. GPT-6.1 Sol helps developers build features, debug issues, investigate complex codebases, and complete multistep workflows. Established AWS controls help you secure workloads, govern access, and audit model invocation activity. You can get started in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions, endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles, and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation .

title: Oracle Database@AWS supports aggregate and default routes for ODB peering
body: Oracle Database@AWS (ODB) now supports advertising aggregate routes and a default route (0.0.0.0/0) when configuring ODB peering between applications in an Amazon VPC and databases in an ODB network. This simplifies network operations as customers extend new VPCs or on-premises networks to reach their databases, without updating the advertised CIDRs for each network that needs connectivity to the ODB network. Previously, customers had to advertise each network reaching the ODB network as a separate CIDR, and could not advertise a broad aggregate range or a default route. With this launch, customers can advertise any CIDR range, so a single aggregate or default route can cover all networks reachable through the peered VPC, such as those connected through an AWS Transit Gateway, without a separate entry for each one. This capability is available on ODB networks that support multiple ODB peering connections, in all AWS Regions where Oracle Database@AWS is available. To learn more, visit Oracle Database@AWS and the Oracle Database@AWS User Guide . To get started, subscribe through AWS Marketplace .

title: Quick now supports smart approvals for agentic actions
body: Amazon Quick now supports smart approvals, a review layer that reduces unnecessary approval prompts while preserving human oversight of the actions that matter most. As agents take more actions on a user's behalf, such as sending email, updating records, and creating tickets, asking a person to approve every step leads to approval fatigue and weaker oversight over time. With smart approvals, a separate review model called the classifier evaluates each eligible action against the user's request. It approves routine actions automatically and refers consequential actions to the user for review. Your existing policies always come first. Smart approvals only reviews actions where the user's setting is "ask" each time. Denied actions stay denied, and smart approvals never grants new access. The classifier sends higher-impact actions to the user for review. These include sending content outside the organization, changing permissions, deleting content, making payments, and actions that go beyond what the user asked for. Each automatic approval covers only the exact action that was reviewed. If a review fails or times out, the action goes to the user. Smart approvals is on for all users by default. Administrators control who can use it with custom permissions, and users can turn it off for their conversations and scheduled runs in chat options. AWS CloudTrail records each action review made through smart approvals and each change to a user's smart approvals setting. Smart approvals is available in Amazon Quick in all AWS Regions where Amazon Quick agentic capabilities are supported. For more information, see the AWS Region table . To learn more about smart approvals, see smart approvals in the Amazon Quick User Guide. For more information about Amazon Quick, see the Amazon Quick product page .

title: Amazon Redshift adds support for creating and refreshing Apache Iceberg materialized views
body: Amazon Redshift now supports the creation and refresh of Apache Iceberg materialized views. Materialized views pre-compute expensive joins and aggregations once and store the results in an Apache Iceberg table in Amazon S3 or Amazon S3 table buckets, registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Materialized views are created using familiar SQL — CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... USING ICEBERG and the results are instantly queryable by any Iceberg-compatible engine, including Amazon Athena, Apache Spark on Amazon EMR and AWS Glue, and third-party engines such as Trino, or Snowflake. Redshift keeps them current by recomputing only what has changed with manual incremental refresh, and because the results are Iceberg tables in the Glue Data Catalog, they are governed and discovered like any other catalog table. Data teams often build analytics in stages, stitching together different engines to clean and transform raw data before serving it. This adds pipeline orchestration overhead and can introduce semantic differences between engines. Iceberg materialized views deliver value in two ways. First, instead of hundreds of users and teams re-running the same expensive joins and aggregations, and re-scanning source tables on every query, you compute the result once and everyone reads the precomputed table. Second, you can run an end-to-end pipeline using a single engine like Apache Spark and now Amazon Redshift, and every downstream consumer shares the same open result without the overhead of orchestrating multiple engines. Either way, the output is an open Iceberg table that any engine can read without copies or conversion. You can still load these tables into Redshift Managed Storage (RMS) as native RMS materialized views for your most performance-sensitive dashboards. You can create Iceberg Materialized Views in any region where Redshift Serverless and provisioned Graviton instances are supported. To learn more, see Materialized views stored as Apache Iceberg tables in the Amazon Redshift Database Developer Guide, the CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW command reference, and the Materialize once, query anywhere blog post.

title: Announcing DNS analytics and insights for Route 53 Global Resolver and DNS Firewall
body: Route 53 Global Resolver and DNS Firewall now provide DNS analytics and insights through native Amazon CloudWatch integration. These new capabilities enable network administrators and security teams to gain full observability into DNS query patterns, monitor DNS Firewall rule effectiveness, detect anomalous activity, and optimize DNS infrastructure performance. DNS analytics and insights is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudWatch, Route 53 Global Resolver, and DNS Firewall are available. With CloudWatch Metrics and Contributor Insights, customers can search and analyze DNS query logs, create metric filters for specific patterns such as blocked queries and DNS response codes, and set automated alarms. A new Analytics tab in both the Global Resolver and DNS Firewall consoles provides streamlined access to all analytics in one place. For example, customers can create a metric filter for blocked DNS queries by VPC and set an alarm to trigger when more than 10 queries are blocked within an hour, enabling rapid response to potential security threats. Standard Amazon CloudWatch pricing applies to the metrics that customers opt in to. To learn more, visit the Route 53 documentation .

title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports custom Tooling blueprints
body: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports custom Tooling blueprints, giving domain administrators the ability to define the foundation of every project by using their own AWS CloudFormation templates. Administrators can tailor project environments to meet organization-specific requirements, such as IAM role names that comply with company naming standards or custom permissions boundaries instead of AWS managed policies. Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio administrators start by authoring a CloudFormation template that describes the project environment they need, then register it as a custom Tooling blueprint. The service validates the template at registration and again after each project deployment, confirming that the required resources exist before any team member uses the project. Templates can include any CloudFormation-supported resource, such as AWS Lake Formation grants, Amazon Athena workgroups, or VPC security groups, and work across multiple AWS accounts and Regions without per-project edits. At deployment time, the service automatically populates reserved template parameters, such as the project ID and domain ID, so administrators define the template once and apply it everywhere. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available. To learn more, visit the Custom blueprints as Tooling documentation .

title: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports the Cyber Risk Institute profile version 2.2
body: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports automated security checks that align with the Cyber Risk Institute (CRI) profile. The CRI Profile is a cybersecurity framework developed by the Cyber Risk Institute, a non-profit coalition of financial institutions and trade associations. The framework harmonizes cybersecurity and regulatory expectations that apply to the financial services sector into a common set of requirements, so that an organization can assess itself once and report against multiple regulations. AWS Security Hub CSPM provides 404 controls that support a subset of CRI Profile v2.2 requirements; the controls don't support requirements that require manual checks. The new standard is now available in all AWS Regions where Security Hub CSPM is currently available, including the AWS GovCloud (US) and the China Regions. To quickly enable the standard across your AWS environment, we recommend that you use Security Hub central configuration. With this approach, you can enable the standard in all or only some of your organization's accounts and across all AWS Regions that are linked to Security Hub with a single action. To learn more, see CRI Profile v2.2 in the AWS Security Hub CSPM user guide. To receive notifications about new Security Hub CSPM features and controls subscribe to the Security Hub SNS topic . You can also try Security Hub CSPM at no cost for 30 days with the AWS Free Tier offering.

title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio adds light mode support for IDC-based domains
body: Today, AWS announces light mode support in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio for Identity Center (IDC) based domains. Customers can now configure the visual interface mode to match their preference, choosing between dark and light themes. With this launch, customers can set this visual preference in both IAM-based and IDC-based domains. Light mode helps improve readability in bright environments and provides a familiar visual experience for customers who prefer lighter interfaces. Combined with the existing dark mode, this update gives you full control over the appearance of your development environment, improving accessibility and reducing eye strain across varying lighting conditions. In SageMaker Unified Studio settings, you can choose 'Customize appearance' under your Profile settings to select between visual modes including dark mode, light mode, and device setting, which matches your operating system's setting. The setting persists across browsers and devices. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available. To learn more, see the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio User Guide.

title: Introducing time series collections for the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
body: Today, we're announcing support for time series collections on the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. With time series collections, you can ingest, store, and analyze logs, metrics, traces, and event data without provisioning or managing clusters. They absorb ingest spikes automatically, keep recent data fast to query, and make months or years of history searchable at low cost, all in the same collection. Time series collections add a new, lower-cost warm storage tier in addition to the existing hot storage tier, so customers can retain their infrequently accessed data without paying hot storage prices. Customers can choose how long data stays hot before transitiong to warm storage. With up to 100 TB of hot storage per collection, time series collections can handle high-volume observability workloads such as application monitoring, security analytics, and IoT telemetry. Alerting and anomaly detection are also now available, so customers can get notified about issues and spot unusual patterns in their log and event data without separate tooling. Time series collections are available today in all AWS Regions where OpenSearch Serverless is available. To learn more about the pricing for the new warm storage, see OpenSearch Serverless pricing . To learn more about time series collections on Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, see the OpenSearch Serverless feature page , the launch blog , and the AWS documentation .

title: AWS Transfer Family now supports custom CloudWatch log groups for managed workflows
body: AWS Transfer Family now lets you choose a custom log group in Amazon CloudWatch Logs for managed workflow execution logs. You can organize workflow logs to monitor individual workflows separately or bring logs from related workflows together. Previously, every workflow attached to a Transfer Family server sent its execution logs to that server’s CloudWatch log group, so you could not set a separate log destination for each workflow. When creating a workflow through the AWS Transfer Family console or API, you can now select a workflow-level log group that is separate from the server’s log group. Transfer Family delivers workflow logs only to the selected group, so no server logging role is required. Workflow logs retain their existing structured JSON format and remain queryable using Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights. You can also send logs from multiple workflows to a shared log group to create consolidated metrics and dashboards for tracking workflow execution. If you do not select a structured log destination, workflow logs continue using the server’s role-based logging configuration when configured. Existing workflows continue using their current logging configuration. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Transfer Family managed workflows are offered. To learn more, visit the Transfer Family managed workflows User Guide .

title: AWS Transfer Family console supports SVG logos and ICO favicons for web apps
body: The AWS Transfer Family console now supports SVG files for logos and ICO files for favicons in web apps, with upload limits increased to 2 MB. This gives you more flexibility to use existing branding assets when customizing your web app. Previously, the console accepted only JPG and PNG files and limited logo uploads to 50 KB and favicon uploads to 20 KB. The console automatically resizes images and converts them to JPG or PNG before saving them. Existing API upload limits and format requirements remain unchanged. These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where Transfer Family web apps are offered. To learn more, see the Transfer Family web apps tutorial .

title: Amazon WorkSpaces simplifies secure AI agent access to enterprise cloud desktops with less infrastructure to operate and manage
body: WorkSpaces for AI agents now handles authentication and desktop connections as part of the managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) service, so you can connect agents to governed cloud desktops, removing the need to write custom code. This makes it easy to use WorkSpaces with any client that supports MCP. Connecting an agent to a desktop previously required you to manage presession requirements; generate, invoke, and rotate streaming URLs manually, adding complexity every time a session expired. You can now create sessions with your existing AWS credentials through OAuth 2.0, and the service handles the connection lifecycle. You configure once which desktop stack to use, and your agents reach the right desktop without ever seeing or handling the underlying streaming connection. You can also query session state to see which desktop stack, fleet, and session an agent is connected to, and generate a link for real-time observability of your agent. This gives you visibility and auditability over active agent work to know what your agents are doing and where. To help your agents work with multiple applications, they can now discover and launch applications through a catalog MCP Tool rather than navigating menus. Using these new tools, agents can list the available applications, launch one or several at runtime, and switch between them, replacing the start-menu and taskbar navigation with a programmatic, deterministic path that improves accuracy and reduces token cost. WorkSpaces for AI agents runs agent sessions inside the same network isolation and compliance boundaries that govern your human workforce, inheriting the VPC controls, data-loss prevention policies, and session-level security posture that enterprises have already configured. The service is also now available in four additional AWS Regions: South America (São Paulo), Europe (Milan), Europe (Spain), and Asia Pacific (Malaysia). To get started operating AI agents on WorkSpaces, visit: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appstream2/latest/developerguide/agent-access.html .

title: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler now provides a higher default quota for the CreateSchedule API
body: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler now has a higher default service quota for the CreateSchedule API action. The default CreateSchedule request rate quota is now 5,000 requests per second in 11 AWS Regions. Quotas can be further increased to tens of thousands of requests per second by making a request through the Service Quotas console. EventBridge Scheduler is a serverless scheduler that allows you to create, run, and manage billions of scheduled events and tasks, across more than 270 AWS services, without provisioning or managing the underlying infrastructure. EventBridge Scheduler supports one-time and recurring schedules that can be created using cron expressions, rate expressions, or specific times with support for time zones and daylight savings. With today's increase to the default CreateSchedule quota, customers with high-throughput schedule creation workloads can operate at increased scale without needing to request a quota increase, reducing friction when onboarding new workloads or scaling existing ones. Scheduler will scale to the new quota automatically. You can request increases beyond the new default service quota in the Service Quotas console. View EventBridge Scheduler service quotas for each Region in the service endpoints and quotas documentation or learn more about the EventBridge Scheduler service in the EventBridge Scheduler documentation . The increased quota is now available in the US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), South America (São Paulo), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Singapore), and Asia Pacific (Sydney) Regions.

title: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) Serverless is now available on DocumentDB 8.0
body: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) Serverless, an on-demand, auto-scaling configuration for DocumentDB, is now available on version 8.0. Amazon DocumentDB Serverless automatically scales capacity up or down in fine-grained increments based on your application's demand, offering up to 90% cost savings compared to provisioning for peak capacity. DocumentDB 8.0 improves query latency by up to 7x and compression ratio by up to 5x, while adding compatibility with MongoDB API versions 6.0, 7.0, and 8.0. It also introduces enhanced vector search with up to 30x faster index builds, new aggregation stages and operators, and support for collation and views. DocumentDB Serverless is available for both new and existing clusters on Amazon DocumentDB 8.0. You can use the in-place major version upgrade (MVU) to convert your Amazon DocumentDB 5.0 clusters to Amazon DocumentDB 8.0 clusters. Please see upgrading your DocumentDB cluster to learn more. To learn more about the regions Amazon DocumentDB Serverless is available, see the supported instance classes by region . To learn more about Amazon DocumentDB Serverless, see the overview , documentation , and AWS News blog

title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports disaggregated prefill and decode
body: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports Disaggregated Prefill and Decode (DPD), an inference optimization that separates the two phases of large language model (LLM) inference — prefill and decode — onto dedicated GPU pools and transfers the key-value (KV) cache between them over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) using GPU-Direct RDMA. Customers running LLMs in production for chat assistants, agentic pipelines, retrieval-augmented generation, and long-document analysis need consistent per-token latency and predictable throughput under mixed traffic, but when prefill and decode share the same GPU, a single long-context request can stall token generation for every concurrent request and force customers to over-provision one phase to protect the other. With DPD, customers run compute-bound prefill on one set of GPUs and memory-bandwidth-bound decode on another, so the two phases no longer contend for the same resources. This delivers more consistent per-token latency under sustained concurrency, higher goodput at strict latency SLOs, and the ability to scale prefill and decode capacity independently to match the input and output distribution of the workload. An intelligent router automatically directs long-context requests through the disaggregated path and sends shorter prompts directly to the decoder, so customers get the benefit on the traffic that needs it without paying transfer overhead on short prompts. Customers enable DPD by adding a `pdSpec` section to the same `InferenceEndpointConfig` custom resource they already use for inference endpoints on the HyperPod Inference Operator, and DPD is composable with the existing KV cache offloading and intelligent routing features on HyperPod. DPD is available for SageMaker HyperPod clusters using the EKS orchestrator on EFA-capable instance types in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available. To learn more, see Disaggregated Prefill and Decode for HyperPod inference in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide.

title: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) clusters now support up to 256 TiB of storage volume
body: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) now supports a maximum storage limit of 256 TiB, doubling the previous limit of 128 TiB. This enhancement allows customers to store and manage even larger datasets within a single DocumentDB cluster, simplifying data management for large-scale applications and supporting the growing data needs of modern applications. Customers only pay for the storage they use, with no need for upfront provisioning of the full 256 TiB. To access the increased storage limit, upgrade your cluster to supported engine versions. Once upgraded, DocumentDB storage will automatically scale up to 256 TiB capacity based on the amount of data in the cluster volume. Visit technical documentation to learn more about supported versions. This new storage volume capacity is available in all AWS regions where Amazon DocumentDB is available. Amazon DocumentDB is a serverless, fully managed, MongoDB API-compatible document database service. It provides built-in security, continuous backups, up to 15 read replicas, Global Clusters for automated multi-Region replication, and integrations with other AWS services. To get started with Amazon DocumentDB, take a look at our getting started page .

title: AWS PrivateLink announces Tunnel Endpoints to access network segments
body: AWS PrivateLink customers can now use VPC endpoint to privately and securely access network segments in another VPC/account. They can use a ‘tunnel’ endpoint, a new type of VPC endpoint, to tunnel into the network segment and access resources located within it. AWS PrivateLink is a highly available and scalable technology that enables private access across VPC and account boundaries to load balanced services, appliances, and resources such as databases and domains. Prior to this launch, customers who wanted to share their resources with another party such as an external vendor had to do it one at a time by creating a Resource Configuration for every resource. Now, customers can create a Resource Configuration to represent a CIDR range in their network, and share it with a vendor via AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM). The vendor can then create a tunnel endpoint and use GENEVE encapsulation to tunnel through it into the customer’s VPC to access resources located in CIDR range specified by the customer. There is an hourly charge for the tunnel endpoint and a per-GB charge for data processed through it. Please refer to the pricing page for AWS PrivateLink . The capability is available in the following AWS Regions : US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), Asia Pacific (Jakarta), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Melbourne), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Osaka), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Canada West (Calgary), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Milan), Europe (Paris), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), Europe (Zurich), Mexico (Central), South America (São Paulo). To learn more about this capability and get started, please refer to the AWS PrivateLink documentation .
